age of the Bangalore Water Supply precedent
when the Industrial Relations Code came into force

articles.body:
Two headlines ran on this judgment on Thursday and they appeared to contradict each other: one said the Supreme Court had scrapped the worker-friendly 1978 precedent, the other that it had kept labour protections intact. Both are partially right, which is the point of the ruling.

**What was at stake.** In *Bangalore Water Supply and Sewerage Board v. A. Rajappa* (1978), a seven-judge Bench led by Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer gave the word "industry" in Section 2(j) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, an expansive reading. It laid down the Triple Test — an activity qualifies if it is systematic or organised, operates on employer-employee cooperation, and produces goods or services to satisfy human wants. That brought hospitals, educational institutions and municipalities inside the definition, exempting only core sovereign functions like the judiciary, law and order and defence. Being an "industry" is what gives workers access to the Act's machinery: collective bargaining, protection against unfair labour practices, and the dispute-resolution route.

**What the nine-judge Bench led by Chief Justice Surya Kant actually held.** By a 5:4 majority, the Court declined to disturb the Triple Test for disputes under the now-repealed Industrial Disputes Act. Workers in pending cases continue to be covered, and government bodies cannot claim an automatic exemption. The Court said the 1978 framework has "stood the test of time", though certain aspects of the test and its guidelines could be refined — and any such reformulation applies prospectively, so already-decided cases are not reopened.

Separately, the majority held that "industry" under Section 2(p) of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, which came into force in November 2025, will not be "burdened" by the 1978 interpretation of Section 2(j). Chief Justice Kant said the earlier judgment will not act as the "sheet anchor" for interpreting the new provision, effectively confining it to legacy disputes pending before courts, tribunals and labour authorities prior to the IRC. That opinion was supported by Justices Satish Chandra Sharma, Alok Aradhe and Vipul M. Pancholi, with Justices P.S. Narasimha and Joymalya Bagchi agreeing in separate opinions.

**Why this is not a clean win for either side.** Workers with live disputes under the old Act keep everything. Employers get a clean slate for the new regime. And the question that actually determines the next two decades of Indian labour litigation — whether hospitals, universities, non-profits and welfare bodies are "industries" under the 2020 Code — is left open, to be decided on the Code's own language and framework in future cases. A nine-judge Bench sat for this and deliberately declined to answer the forward-looking question.

**The practical effect.** Expect a wave of litigation testing Section 2(p) institution by institution, and expect employers to argue that the new Code's language is narrower by design. Expect unions to argue that Parliament legislated against the backdrop of 48 years of settled interpretation and cannot be presumed to have silently abandoned it. Both arguments are now open in a way they were not on Wednesday.

**What it means for an Indian investor.** The four labour codes were sold as a deregulation package, and this ruling removes a significant interpretive constraint on one of them — a modest positive for employers in healthcare, education and services, and for the labour-cost assumptions underlying those sectors. But the uncertainty cuts the other way for planning: a company cannot yet know whether its workforce falls inside or outside the Code's dispute machinery. Sectors with large contract and outsourced workforces — hospitals, IT services, logistics, facilities management — carry the most exposure to how Section 2(p) is eventually read.

**What to watch.** The full text of the majority and the four dissents, the first High Court cases interpreting Section 2(p), and whether the government issues clarificatory rules rather than waiting for litigation.

articles.title: Startup funding stays narrow: Peeko takes $7mn, BGauss ₹110 crore, and two fintechs post real revenue

Orange Health FY26 revenue, +65%, with ~₹100 cr loss

articles.body:
Four Indian startup disclosures landed within 24 hours, and read together they describe a funding market that is functioning but narrow.

**Peeko — ₹67.4 crore ($7mn+) Series A, led by Chiratae Ventures.** The Bengaluru babycare quick-commerce platform, founded last year by Chetan Sharma, Abhijit Gairola and Vivek Khetan, delivers baby and kids' essentials in 60 minutes. Existing investor Stellaris Venture Partners participated, having led a $3.2 million round last August. The operating detail: three dark stores in Bengaluru covering about 55% of the city, expanding to six by end-2026 and two more cities next year; assortment grown from ~6,000 SKUs at launch to 27,000-30,000; average order value around ₹1,000; more than one lakh parents having shopped since launch; claimed near-doubling every quarter for six months. Proceeds go toward a broader "parenting partner" proposition alongside commerce. The ₹1,000 AOV is the number that makes this different from grocery quick commerce — apparel, toys and baby gear carry margins that ₹300 grocery baskets do not.

**BGauss — ₹110 crore ($11.6mn) Series D at a ₹1,000-1,100 crore post-money valuation.** Read the cap table before the headline. Founder Hemant Mahendrakumar Kabra led the round himself with ₹50 crore; existing investor Bharat Value Fund put in ₹44 crore; Adesh Realtor LLP ₹10 crore and Maithan Alloys ₹6 crore. The board approved 17,26,846 Series D CCPS at ₹637 per share. That is an insider round with no new institutional lead — the founder is funding his own company. The operating context explains why: 5,518 retail registrations in July 2026, roughly 3x year-on-year growth, but a 0.3% share of India's electric two-wheeler market, against Ather, River Mobility, Ola Electric, Hero MotoCorp, TVS and Bajaj. Tripling from a small base in a market with well-capitalised incumbents is a hard pitch to a new investor.

**Phi Commerce — ₹38.54 crore (~$4mn) ongoing Series B, entirely from existing investors.** The Pune omnichannel payments firm, whose PayPhi platform handles online, in-store, on-the-go and doorstep transactions, is issuing 57,065 Series B CCPS at ₹6,754.81 each. Entrackr estimates the valuation at around ₹1,505 crore, up from ₹1,361 crore. A ~10% valuation step-up on a small insider round, roughly a year after raising $11 million across two rounds from BEENEXT and DG Strategic Investment. Founders Jose Thattil, Anil Sharma, Tushar Shankar and Rajesh Londhe collectively retain 33.7%.

**The FY26 financials are the more interesting half.** Cashfree Payments, after a flat FY25, grew operating revenue 51% to ₹967 crore from ₹640 crore, with losses narrowing 23%. Payment gateway commissions drove it, jumping 85% to ₹890 crore; payouts contributed ₹69 crore and cross-border ₹8 crore. Processing costs — 64% of expenses — rose 66% to ₹698 crore, employee costs edged down to ₹239 crore, and marketing fell 10% to ₹18 crore. That combination — revenue up 51% with marketing down 10% — is the signature of a business growing on distribution rather than spend. It holds all three RBI payments licences (PA-PG, PA-CB, PPI) and processes over $80 billion annually.

Orange Health Labs grew revenue 65% to ₹138.6 crore but widened losses to nearly ₹100 crore while expanding across tier-1 cities, adding 60+ company-owned collection centres, nearly 50 in Bengaluru. It is raising $30 million, which will show up in FY27.

**What it means for an Indian investor.** The pattern is capital concentrating in businesses with visible unit economics — Cashfree's narrowing loss, Peeko's ₹1,000 AOV — while everything else takes insider money at flat-to-modest step-ups. For public-market investors, Cashfree's numbers are a useful private-market comparable for listed payments and fintech names.

It had $8 billion in cash but spent $5.7 billion on equipment in one quarter.
Fund managers in Asia now say US long-term interest rates are the main thing driving AI stocks.
The reason: AI companies now fund their buildout with debt instead of profits.

articles.body:
Nebius Group upsized its debt offering on Wednesday to $5 billion from $4.5 billion — $3 billion of private convertible notes maturing in 2030 and $2 billion maturing in 2034, with purchasers able to take an additional $450 million and $300 million respectively. Proceeds go to expanding data-centre capacity, investing in its full-stack AI cloud platform, and acquiring GPUs and other components. Alongside the offering the Amsterdam-headquartered company said it would separately exchange $800 million of debt for about 15.8 million Class A shares with certain noteholders. Its shares closed nearly 10% lower.

**The balance-sheet arithmetic.** Nebius ended June with $8.04 billion in cash and cash equivalents. It spent $5.66 billion on property, equipment and intangible assets in the second quarter alone. At that burn rate the cash pile funds under a year and a half of capacity expansion, which is why the raise happened and why it was upsized. The 10% share fall is the market pricing the dilution and the leverage against the growth the capacity is supposed to deliver.

**Why this specific deal is the whole AI-financing story in miniature.** Two years ago hyperscale AI capacity was funded from the operating cash flow of extremely profitable incumbents. It increasingly is not. Alibaba, reporting the same day, showed capex up 75% to 67.7 billion yuan with free cash *outflow* of 44.7 billion yuan. Nebius is issuing convertibles. Across the sector, funding has shifted from free cash flow to debt financing — and that changes what the asset class is.

**The consequence, stated plainly by the people trading it.** Stock traders in mainland China and Hong Kong are now looking to the US bond market for cues on whether the AI trade is sustainable. "Rising US Treasury yields put pressure on valuations across risk assets," said He Siyao, a fund manager at HSBC Jintrust Fund Management. "For equities, AI is becoming more sensitive to the interest rate, because industry funding shifts from free cash flow to debt financing. With valuations under pressure, that will also cloud the earnings outlook and increase the volatility of the AI sector."

This week gave that thesis a live test. Fears of a debt-issuance glut drove the US 30-year yield to a nearly two-decade high of 5.32-5.34% and the 10-year to levels last seen in early 2025, with bond investors demanding more term premium for the supply. Two sources of that supply: the US government funding its deficit, and the hyperscalers expanding bond borrowing to finance the AI buildout. Then the Treasury doubled its long-bond buybacks, yields fell, and risk assets — including AI names, gold and bitcoin — rallied. The chain from a Treasury operations announcement to an AI stock price is now three links long and fully visible.

**The uncomfortable circularity.** AI companies borrow to build capacity. Their borrowing contributes to the supply glut that raises long-term yields. Higher long-term yields raise their own cost of capital and compress the valuations that justify the buildout. Sygnum's Max Stuedlein made the point explicitly, describing borrowing costs as rising on US debt levels and "partial crowding out by debt issuances of hyperscalers". This does not have to end badly — depreciation schedules are long and utilisation could justify everything — but it is a feedback loop, and feedback loops are how funding markets turn.

**What it means for an Indian investor.** If you hold global technology exposure through international funds or ETFs, your dominant risk factor right now is the US long end, not AI product cycles. Domestically, India's own data-centre buildout — including L&T's NVIDIA B300 AI Factory order — is being financed in the same global capital market, so the cost of that capacity is set in New York regardless of where the servers sit.

**What to watch.** The pricing and conversion terms on the Nebius notes, whether other AI-cloud issuers follow, and the 30-year Treasury yield as the sector's real benchmark.
